title: On AI becoming a crutch for students
author: Paul Matthews
summary: Paul Matthews reframes the common objection to AI use in schools—that it will become a 'crutch'—by arguing that crutches are sometimes exactly what a student needs. Using the analogy of a marathon runner with a rolled ankle who can only move forward with crutch support, Matthews argues that students with chronic literacy deficits or cognitive challenges are already struggling in ways invisible to their classmates, and that AI scaffolding—text simplification, writing prompts, retrieval practice generation—allows them to participate in learning rather than drowning silently. He trains his students to use three AI-assisted strategies: using AI to simplify complex texts, generate writing prompts, and create retrieval practice quizzes. His central point is not that all students should use AI as a substitute for thinking, but that the 'cognitive crutch' framing is too binary—the same tool that would be an avoidance mechanism for a high-performing student may be the only path to engagement for a student with a literacy deficit. The article ends with a genuine question rather than a fixed answer, inviting readers to identify where on the spectrum of 'firm no / yes but / heck yes' they fall.
points: The crutch metaphor cuts in both directions: a crutch is an appropriate intervention for someone who is injured and cannot walk without it, and dismissing AI scaffolding as always bad is analogous to refusing to give a crutch to a runner with a rolled ankle.

The students most likely to benefit from AI as a scaffold are the ones hardest to reach through conventional differentiation: students with chronic literacy deficits who 'wear the same uniform and sit in the same classroom' but intellectually cannot keep pace.

Three high-leverage AI uses for struggling students: simplifying complex texts while preserving structure and flagging key vocabulary; generating writing prompts for reflection or analysis; creating retrieval practice quizzes and study materials on demand.

The monitored, purposeful use of AI as a scaffold is categorically different from cognitive outsourcing: the distinction lies in whether the tool is reducing cognitive load to enable learning or replacing the cognition that learning requires.

The question of whether AI is a crutch or a scaffold is not answerable in the abstract—it depends entirely on the student, the task, and the degree of independence that student needs to be developing toward.
quotes: With the help of the crutch, the athlete was able to make his way out of the cobbled streets of Old Town and back to his accommodation. The crutch wasn't holding him back. It was the only thing helping him forward.

Consider a chronic literacy deficit. Someone like Jess, a year 9 student who is great value but really struggles academically. Jess may wear the same uniform and sit in the same classroom as her friends, but intellectually she just can't keep pace.

In an ideal world, teachers would have all the time in the world to differentiate, personalise, and work one-to-one. But we face the immutable reality of being limited to one place at any one time and having only 24 hours in a day.

Act as a language tutor. Simplify the reading level of this text. Give me a one paragraph executive summary at the top. Then reproduce the whole text, keeping the same structure and headings, but simplifying the language and providing a simple vocabulary at the end.

Just as we can admit there is an appropriate use for a physical crutch, can we not also admit there are appropriate uses for a cognitive crutch? Could it help a struggling student walk with her classmates through the learning for that week?
Of course their use needs to be monitored. Of course we need to encourage them to pursue rigour and not meander down the path of least resistance.
